blocks.text: Quick verdict

Rayobyte is the better value at volume: at 100 GB it costs about $200 against Decodo's $275, and from a terabyte its rate drops to $0.90/GB, with traffic that never expires. Decodo is the better choice for teams that need SOCKS5 (Rayobyte's residential gateway is HTTP(S) only), ZIP or ASN targeting, a free trial, or scraping APIs for harder targets, and its 115M+ pool is clearly published. At 10 GB the two cost the same, so let features decide small purchases.

Decodo and Rayobyte both sell residential, datacenter, ISP and mobile proxies at mid-market prices, and both are popular with scraping teams in the 10-500 GB a month range. Decodo offers a larger published pool, SOCKS5 and scraping APIs. Rayobyte offers residential traffic that never expires and some of the steepest volume discounts on the market. This comparison works out which model is cheaper at your volume and which feature gaps matter.

blocks.text: Decodo in 2026: what you get

Decodo is the 2024 rebrand of Smartproxy, one of the most popular mid-market providers. Its residential network is advertised at 115 million IPs across 195+ locations, and independent benchmarks put its success rate around 99.9% with sub-second response times. Every plan includes the full pool plus city, state, ZIP and ASN targeting, and the dashboard is one of the easiest to set up. Decodo also sells datacenter, ISP and mobile proxies and a family of scraping APIs.

Strengths: Large 115M+ pool at a mid-market price; Near-perfect success rates in independent tests; Clean, fast self-service onboarding; Scraping APIs available when raw proxies are not enough. Weak spots: Plan traffic does not roll over; Published pricing stops at 100 GB; beyond that you need a quote; More expensive per GB than budget brands.
Rayobyte in 2026: what you get

Rayobyte is a US proxy company that started life as Blazing SEO and built its name on dedicated datacenter proxies. Residential proxies have since become its main product. It sells them pay-as-you-go in four volume bands with traffic that never expires, sources at least part of its residential pool in-house, and offers country, region and city targeting. The notable limit is protocol support: its residential gateway does not support SOCKS5 or UDP.

Strengths: Non-expiring residential traffic; Steep volume discounts down to $0.90/GB; Excellent datacenter and ISP catalog; Well-regarded human support. Weak spots: No SOCKS5 or UDP on residential; Pool size not prominently published; Fewer advanced targeting options than enterprise providers.
Pricing: Decodo vs Rayobyte

Decodo sells residential traffic at $4/GB pay-as-you-go with no commitment, or on monthly plans: 3 GB for $11.25 ($3.75/GB), 10 GB for $35, 25 GB at $3.25/GB, 50 GB for $150 and 100 GB for $275 ($2.75/GB). Top-ups are billed at your plan's rate, so you are not pushed into the next tier.
Rayobyte prices residential traffic in four pay-as-you-go bands: $3.50/GB for 1-49 GB, $2/GB for 50-249 GB, $1.50/GB for 250-999 GB and $0.90/GB for 1-5 TB. Traffic does not expire.

At 10 GB a month the two cost almost the same: about $35 with Decodo against $35 with Rayobyte. Buying 100 GB, you would pay about $200 with Rayobyte and $275 with Decodo: a 27% saving in Rayobyte's favour. Look past the per-GB figure too. Rayobyte lets unused traffic carry forward, while Decodo's allowance does not (plan traffic resets monthly; payg for bursty work). For irregular workloads, that difference can outweigh a small gap in list price.
Pool size, coverage and targeting

Rayobyte does not publish a clear residential pool figure, so a size comparison is not possible on published data. Decodo lists '115M+' and Rayobyte lists 'Not prominently published'. In practice, what matters is how many unique IPs you get in the countries you target, which you can measure in a short trial by sending a few thousand requests and counting distinct exit addresses. For coverage, Decodo lists 195+ countries and Rayobyte lists Global. On targeting, Decodo offers country, state, city, ZIP and ASN, while Rayobyte offers country, region and city.
Protocols, sessions and setup

Protocol support is a real difference here. Decodo supports HTTP, HTTPS, SOCKS5, while Rayobyte offers HTTP, HTTPS (no SOCKS5 on residential). If your tooling needs SOCKS5, for example some anti-detect browsers, desktop apps or non-HTTP traffic, that settles it in Decodo's favour. On sessions, Decodo offers rotating or sticky sessions with configurable duration, and Rayobyte offers rotates per request by default; sticky sessions available. Setup works the same way on both: a single gateway endpoint, with location and session options passed as username parameters, plus IP whitelisting if you prefer not to use credentials.
Which is better for your use case?
General web scraping: Decodo. Decodo has the edge here. Why: a large pool and near-perfect benchmark success rates. How Rayobyte compares: cheap volume bands and traffic that never expires.
SERP and rank tracking: Decodo wins. The deciding factor for Decodo: a dedicated SERP scraping API plus city targeting. The limitation on the Rayobyte side: usable, with no dedicated SERP product.
Social media and multi-account management: Decodo. Decodo has the edge here. Why: sticky sessions, sub-users and an easy dashboard. How Rayobyte compares: no SOCKS5 limits some account tools.

E-commerce price and stock monitoring: close call. Both are reasonable choices here. Decodo: ZIP targeting and a ready-made e-commerce API. Rayobyte: city targeting and low prices at volume. Let price and the countries you need decide.
Ad verification and geo-testing: Decodo. Decodo has the edge here. Why: wide coverage with city and ASN targeting. How Rayobyte compares: fewer carrier or ASN controls.
Tight budgets: Rayobyte. Rayobyte has the edge here. Why: $2/GB from 50 GB and $0.90/GB at a terabyte. How Decodo compares: it is mid-priced, not cheap.
Trials, verification and billing fine print

Before you pay, check how each provider lets you test. Decodo: Free trial (about 100 MB) on residential. Rayobyte: Check current offer. Verification and payment rules differ too. Decodo: Light KYC; checks on some targets. Rayobyte: Standard verification; US company. Whichever you choose, measure cost per successful request rather than cost per gigabyte: retries, blocked pages and heavy page assets all burn bandwidth, and a cheaper network that fails more often can end up costing more. Blocking images and fonts in your scraper, reusing sessions where a target allows it, and capping concurrency are the quickest ways to cut the bill on either provider.
How to test Decodo and Rayobyte before you commit
The quickest way to choose between Decodo and Rayobyte is a side-by-side test on the sites and countries you actually care about:
1. Buy the smallest option on each side (Decodo: free trial (about 100 MB) on residential; Rayobyte: check current offer).
2. Pick three to five real target URLs and the two or three countries that matter most, and send the same number of requests (a few hundred is enough) through each provider at the same time of day.
3. Record success rate, median response time, CAPTCHAs or blocks, and the number of unique exit IPs you received per country.
4. Divide what you spent by the number of successful, correctly located responses to get cost per useful request, then scale that to your monthly volume.
Bottom line

Across the six use cases above, Decodo comes out ahead in 4, Rayobyte in 1, and 1 is a tie. That makes Decodo the safer default if you are unsure, but the right answer still depends on your volume and targets: Decodo is strongest for small and mid-size scraping teams, while Rayobyte is strongest for mid-to-high volume scraping on a budget. If you can, spend a few dollars testing both on the exact sites and countries you care about; a one-hour test tells you more than any spec sheet.
Decodo is the better pick for:
Small and mid-size scraping teams
Developers who want enterprise-like quality without contracts
Mixed workloads that may grow into scraping APIs
Rayobyte is the better pick for:
Mid-to-high volume scraping on a budget
Teams that also need datacenter or ISP IPs
US buyers who want a US-based vendor
